docComment:
/**
 * A levelled console logger for Node.js applications and libraries.
 *
 * @remarks
 *
 * The package exports the `Logger` class, which writes messages to the
 * console from a given log level, and the types of its options. Create a
 * logger with a level, then call its logging methods (`error()`, `warn()`,
 * `info()`, `verbose()`, `debug()`, and `trace()`); a message is written
 * only if the level of the logger is equal to or higher than that of the
 * method.
 *
 * The package is an ES module, and has no runtime dependencies.
 *
 * @packageDocumentation
 */
name: @xpack/logger

members.docComment:
/** * The `Logger` class implements the logger functionality. * * @remarks * * The package is an ES module; CommonJS code can load it with `require()` * on Node.js 22.12 or later. * * The description has sections on the empty messages, the logging methods, * extending the class, the timestamps, the prefix and the expansion of an * `Error`, the untrusted input, and the preliminary state and its cost. * * The logger is constructed on top of a console object, where the * messages are logged. The class has a type parameter, the type of the * console, so that the `console` accessor returns the object that was * passed, with its own type: a `Logger` without a console is a * `Logger`, and a logger constructed with a `MockConsole` is a * `Logger`, whose `console` accessor gives access to the * members of the mock without a cast. The type must have the `log()` and * `error()` functions (see `LoggerConsole`). Since a logger without a * console uses the JavaScript standard `console` object, the console can * be omitted only if that object is of the type `C`; for a richer type, * like `Logger`, it is required, and the compiler rejects the * constructor call without it. * * Use `log.always()` instead of the `console.log()`, since it writes on the * console of the logger, so a test can capture it with a mock console and a * subclass can intercept it with `write()`; in the preliminary state it is * buffered, like the other messages. * * The log levels, from the lowest to the highest, are `silent`, `error`, * `warn`, `info`, `verbose`, `debug`, `trace`, and `all`. A higher level * writes more messages: a message is written when the log level is equal * to or higher than the level of its method. The `error` and `warn` levels * are for problems, `info` and `verbose` for the progress of the * application, `debug` and `trace` for the details needed to diagnose it, * `silent` writes only the messages of `always()`, and `all` writes * everything. * * There is no `critical` level, corresponding to errors that prevent * the program from running, since these are actually related to bugs; * use `assert()` from `node:assert` instead. * * The messages may include formatting directives, with additional * arguments, as defined by the Node.js `Console` (template literals are * often simpler). * * All logging methods accept an optional message, of any type, and * possibly some arguments, as processed by the standard Node.js * {@link https://nodejs.org/api/util.html#utilformatformat-args | util.format()} * function. * * Empty messages. If the message is omitted or `undefined`, it is * replaced by an empty string, so `log.info()` and `log.info(undefined)` * write an empty line, and the methods with a prefix write only the * prefix (for example `debug: `). This differs from `console.log()`, * which writes `undefined`. Other falsy values are written as they are * (`null`, `0`, and `false` give `null`, `0`, and `false`), and * `undefined` is written as usual when it is not the first argument * (`log.info('value:', undefined)` gives `value: undefined`). Since * the empty string is still a message, any further arguments are * appended to it after a space (`log.info(undefined, 1)` gives ` 1`, * with a leading space). To write the text `undefined`, convert it * explicitly, for example `log.info(String(value))`. * * Logging methods. The methods differ by the level from which they * are written (the threshold), by the console stream, and by a prefix * added to the message: * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * * *
MethodWritten from levelStreamPrefix
always()every levelstdoutnone
error()errorstderrerror:
output()errorstdoutnone
warn()warnstderrwarning:
info()infostdoutnone
verbose()verbosestdoutnone
debug()debugstdoutdebug:
trace()tracestdouttrace:
* * Here stdout is `console.log()` and stderr is `console.error()`. A * method is written when the log level is equal to or higher than its * threshold; at `silent` only `always()` is written. The method * `error()` omits its prefix when the first argument is an `Error` * (see below). * * The three methods that write on stdout without a prefix are used for * different purposes: * *
    *
  • always() is for the messages that must be shown at every * log level, including silent, like the version or the result * requested by the user;
    • *
  • output() is for the normal output of the application, * which is suppressed at silent, together with all the other * messages;
    • *
  • info() is for informative messages, shown from the * info level.
    • *
* * Extending the class. A subclass can intercept the messages by * overriding the protected `write()` method, which is the only supported * extension point (see its description for the contract). The state of * the logger is private; use the public members, like `level`, `hasLevel`, * `isLevel()`, and `console`. The protected members that gave direct access * to the state (`_console`, `levelNumericValue`, `levelName`, and * `buffer`) are deprecated, still work, and will be removed in the next * major version. * * Timestamps. If the logger is created with the `timestamp` option, * the messages of the methods that have a prefix start with the local * time, and the prefix is replaced by the kind of the message in square * brackets; the format and the details are in the description of the * `timestamp` accessor. * * Errors. An `Error` passed to a logging method is expanded with its * stack trace and its `cause` chain, and `error()` omits its prefix for it; * the details, and how to show only the message, are in the description of * `error()`. * * Untrusted input. The messages are written as they are, without * any escaping, so text that comes from outside the application (like * a file name, a user name, or the content of a network request) can * forge messages, send control sequences to the terminal, and be * interpreted as format directives: * *
    *
  • a newline in the text starts a new line in the output, and a prefix * is added only to the first line, so the text bob, a newline, * and error: forged in a warn() call writes the * line warning: bob, followed by a line that looks like a * genuine error: forged message;
    • *
  • control characters, like the ANSI escape sequences, are passed to * the terminal unchanged;
    • *
  • if the first argument contains directives (like %s, * %d, or %j) and there are further arguments, the * directives consume them, so log.info(text, secret) may write * the secret; a single argument is not processed * (log.info('100%d') writes 100%d), but * log.info('100%d', 5) writes 1005.
    • *
* * Therefore pass the untrusted text as an argument, never as the first * argument, with a constant format string: * ```javascript * log.info('user: %s', name) * ``` * * This prevents the interpretation of the directives, but `%s` writes a * string as it is, including the newlines and the control characters. To * also escape them, use `%j` (JSON) or `%O` (as `util.inspect()`), which * write the string between quotes, with a newline as `\n` and the * escape character as `\u001b` or `\x1B`: * ```javascript * log.info('user: %j', name) * ``` * * Note that `%j` calls the `toJSON()` method of an object, and that * `%j` and `%O` quote the strings. * * If the logging code is more complex than a single line, * for example if it needs a long loop, * it is recommended to explicitly check the log level and, * if not high enough, skip the code entirely. * ```javascript * if (log.isTraceEnabled) { * for (const [folderName, folder] of Object.entries(folders)) { * log.trace(`'${folderName}' ${folder.toolchainOptions}`) * } * } * ``` * * There are cases when the logger must be created very early in the * life cycle of an application, even before it is practically possible * to determine the log level. * * For these cases, if the logger is created without a log level, * it is in a preliminary state, and all messages are * stored in an internal buffer, until the log * level is set, when the buffer is replayed and the messages are written. * * Nothing is written while the logger is in the preliminary state, not * even the messages of `always()` and `error()`. If the log level is never * set (for example when the application fails before it determines the * level), the buffered messages are never written and are lost. Set the * log level on every path, for example in a `catch` or `finally` block, * using `hasLevel` to check whether it was set: * ```javascript * try { * // Determine the log level, then set it. * log.level = parseLevel(process.argv) * } catch (err) { * if (!log.hasLevel) { * log.level = Logger.recommendedLevel * } * log.error(err) * } * ``` * * The cost of the preliminary state, which formats and stores every message, * is described in the description of `hasLevel`. * * @typeParam C - The type of the console object; the default is the * Node.js `Console`, which is used when no console is passed. * * @example * ```javascript * import { Logger } from '@xpack/logger' * * const log = new Logger({ level: 'info' }) * log.info('Started') // Started * log.debug('Details') // Nothing, since `debug` is above the level. * log.error('Failed') // error: Failed, on the standard error. * ``` * */

members.docComment: /** * Create a Logger instance. * * @remarks * * The typical use case is to create a logger with a given log level, * usually `info`. * ```javascript * const log = new Logger({ * level: 'info' * }) * ``` * * By default, the system console is used. * * The complete use case is to create the logger instance with both a * `console` and a `level`. This might be particularly useful in tests, * where a mock console can be used to capture the messages. * ```javascript * const log = new Logger({ * console: mockConsole, * level: 'info' * }) * ``` * * If present, the `console` must be an object that has the `log()` and * `error()` functions (see `LoggerConsole`), like the Node.js `Console`, * a mock console derived from it, or a minimal `{ log, error }` object. * It can be omitted only if the JavaScript standard `console` object is of * the type `C` of the logger, as for the default `Console` or for a * minimal type; for a richer type, like `Logger`, it is * required. * * The `level` property is optional since it can be set later. * Without it, the constructor will * create the logger in a preliminary state, and all messages will be stored * in an internal buffer until the log level is set. * ```javascript * const log = new Logger() * ``` * * @param args - The optional options object (see `LoggerParams`), which * is required if the `console` of the type `C` is required (see * `LoggerArguments`). * * @throws * * RangeError * If the level is a string that is not one of the valid names. * * @throws * * TypeError * If the level is not a string (a `level` that is `undefined` is * the same as no level), if the `timestamp` option is not a boolean, or if * the console does not have the `log()` and `error()` functions. The level * errors are the same as those of the `level` setter. */

/** * Log an error message, if the log level is `error` or higher. * * @remarks * * The message is prefixed with `error: ` and * passed via `console.error()`. If the logger was created with the * `timestamp` option, it starts with a timestamp, and the prefix is * replaced by `[error]`, also for an `Error` that comes first (see * below). * * The prefix of an Error. Only `error()` omits its * prefix, and only when the first argument is an `Error`: the first line * of the expanded error already starts with its name (like `Error: boom` or * `TypeError: bad`), which tells the severity. This is deliberate. The * other methods keep their prefix (`warning: Error: boom`, * `debug: Error: boom`), since without it a warning would look like an * error, and a debug message like a failure; and an `Error` that is not * the first argument of `error()` keeps the prefix too * (`error: failed: Error: boom`). It is the same for all the methods, * whether the message is written at once or buffered. * * Logging errors. `Error` objects (and objects derived from it) are * expanded by `util.format()`, as by `console.log()`: the first line has * the name and the message (for example `Error: boom`), and it is * followed by the stack trace and, if present, the `cause` chain, on * several lines. This is the same in all logging methods, which differ * only by the stream and the prefix. The caller decides how much of an * error is shown: * *
    *
  • to show the full details, including the stack trace, pass the error * object, for example log.error(err);
    • *
  • to show a single line, pass only its message, for example * log.error(err.message), which outputs * error: boom.
    • *
* * A common pattern, which also works in the preliminary state, is to show * the message at the `error` level, and the full details only when the * log level is `debug` or higher: * ```javascript * try { * // ... * } catch (err) { * // On stderr: `error: boom`. * log.error(err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err)) * // On stdout, only at `debug` or higher: `debug: Error: boom`, * // followed by the stack trace. * log.debug(err) * } * ``` * * In TypeScript, the variable of a `catch` clause has the type `unknown`, * hence the `instanceof` check. To also keep the name of the error, use * `String(err)` instead of `err.message`: `log.error(String(err))` * outputs, for example, `error: TypeError: boom`. * * @param message - Message to log, as accepted by `util.format()` (see * Empty messages in the description of the class). * * @param args - The variable arguments. * * @example * ```javascript * log.error('Not good...') * ``` * */
members.name: error

/** * Check if the log level was set. * * @remarks * * If the logger was created without an explicit log level, the * logger is in a preliminary state and all messages will be stored * in an internal buffer until the log level is set. * * Cost of the preliminary state. With the level set, a message that * is below the level is skipped before it is formatted, which costs a * few nanoseconds (all the times and sizes in this section are indicative, * and depend on the machine and on the Node.js version). In the * preliminary state the final level is not known, so every message, * including `debug()` and `trace()`, is formatted * immediately and stored in the buffer, until the level is set: * *
    *
  • the formatting is done even for the messages that are later * discarded; for example, an object passed to a %o directive * is inspected at each call (a few microseconds, against a * fraction of a microsecond for a short string message);
    • *
  • the buffer is not limited, and a message of about 70 characters * takes several hundred bytes, so a long running application that logs * a lot before the level is set should set it as early as possible;
    • *
  • since the message is formatted when it is logged, a later change of * an argument does not alter the buffered message.
    • *
* * The check of the level before an expensive preparation of the message * (see the example in the description of `Logger`) is true in the * preliminary state, so the preparation is done there too. * *
    *
  • changed to an accessor in v5.0.0
    • *
  • added as a method in v2.1.0
    • *
* * @returns True if the level was set. * * @example * ```javascript * if (!log.hasLevel) { * log.level = Logger.recommendedLevel * } * ``` * */
members.name: hasLevel

 * preliminary state (see `hasLevel`).

 * If the log level that is set is not one of the known strings, an error
 * is thrown (a `TypeError` for a value that is not a string, including
 * `undefined`, and a `RangeError` for a string that is not a level
 * name), with a message that lists the valid names. To validate a level
 * that comes from an unchecked source, like a command line option, use
 * `Logger.isLogLevel()` first; the valid names are in
 * `Logger.levelNames`.
 *
 * If this is the first time when the log level is set, the messages of
 * the internal buffer are replayed.
 *
 * The buffer is emptied before the messages are written, so each
 * buffered message is written at most once. If the console throws
 * while the buffer is replayed, the exception is propagated to the
 * caller, the level remains set, and the buffered messages that were
 * not yet written are discarded.
 *
 * The type of the setter is `LogLevel`, while the getter is
 * `LogLevel | undefined`: the level is `undefined` only in the
 * preliminary state, and cannot be set back to `undefined`.
 *
 * @returns A string with the log level name, as it was set, or
 *  `undefined` in the preliminary state.
 *
 * @example
 * ```javascript
 * log.level = 'info'
 * ```
 *
 * @example
 * ```javascript
 * console.log(log.level)
 * ```
 *
 * @throws
 *
 * TypeError
 * If the level that is set is not a string.
 *
 * @throws
 *
 * RangeError
 * If the level that is set is not one of the valid names.
 */
members.name: level

Without the option, the same messages * start with the prefix, as in `warning: the file is missing`. * * The timestamp and the kind are tied to the method, not to the prefix * that is written: `error()` with an `Error` that comes first has no * prefix without the option, but with the option it has both, as in * `2026-11-11 23:32:31.358 [error] Error: boom`, so all the stamped * messages have the same structure. The messages without a prefix * (`always()`, `output()`, `info()`, and `verbose()`) are the normal output * and the progress messages, and are never stamped. members.docComment:
/**
 * The internal log writer, which subclasses may override.
 *
 * @remarks
 *
 * It is the supported extension point of the class: every message that
 * passes the level check is formatted, prefixed, and passed here, so an
 * override can inspect, change, redirect, or drop it, and call
 * `super.write()` to continue.
 *
 * If the log level was set, `super.write()` calls the actual logger
 * function, otherwise it stores the message in the internal buffer, for
 * later processing, when the log level is finally set (the function is
 * then called when the level is set, if the message passes the level).
 *
 * In the preliminary state the level is not known, so every message is
 * passed here, including those that the level, once set, will discard.
 * `super.write()` stores them in the internal buffer, and the `level`
 * setter filters them, and calls the stored functions directly, without
 * calling `write()` again. An override that does not call
 * `super.write()` must therefore not assume that a message passes the
 * level: when `hasLevel` is true, it can compare `numericLevel` with
 * `Logger.numericLevels[this.level]`.
 *
 * If the message is `undefined`, nothing is written and nothing is
 * stored. The public logging methods always pass a string; the case is
 * part of the contract of this method, for the subclasses that call it
 * directly.
 *
 * @param numericLevel - The log numeric level.
 *
 * @param loggerFunction - The function to be used to write
 *  the message.
 *
 * @param message - The message, already formatted and prefixed, or
 *  `undefined`, when nothing is written or stored.
 *
 * @example
 * ```javascript
 * class CountingLogger extends Logger {
 *   count = 0
 *
 *   write(numericLevel, loggerFunction, message) {
 *     // Also called, in the preliminary state, for the messages that
 *     // the level, once set, will discard.
 *     this.count++
 *     super.write(numericLevel, loggerFunction, message)
 *   }
 * }
 * ```
 *
 */
members.name: write
